claim: Synaptic plasticity distributed across multiple sites of a circuit is thought to underlie changes in behavior.
source: Synaptic plasticity distributed across multiple sites of a circuit is thought to underlie changes in behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's understanding of synaptic plasticity and behavior, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Feedback loops can be internal to the brain, as in the recurrent circuits thought to underlie short-term memory, predictive coding, and gain control.
source: Feedback loops can be internal to the brain — as in the recurrent circuits thought to underlie short-term memory, predictive coding, and gain control (Constantinidis and Wang, 2004; Douglas and Martin, 2007; Fang et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on recurrent circuits.

claim: Feedback loops can be partially external to the brain, arising whenever a behavior influences sensory input from the environment that, in turn, influences subsequent behavior.
source: or partially external to the brain, arising whenever a behavior influences sensory input from the environment that, in turn, influences subsequent behavior, such as during control of movements (Robinson, 1965; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Holst and Mittelstaedt, 1950).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on sensorimotor feedback.

claim: Feedback loops make it challenging to identify the sites of plasticity that underlie learning.
source: Such feedback loops make it challenging to identify the sites of plasticity that underlie learning.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the presence of feedback loops in neural systems.

claim: Direct measurement of synaptic strength is extremely difficult in intact behaving animals.
source: Because direct measurement of synaptic strength is extremely difficult in intact behaving animals
evidence: This represents established knowledge about technical limitations in neuroscience.

claim: A common approach is to infer changes in synaptic strength from observed changes in neural firing.
source: a common approach is to instead infer changes in synaptic strength from observed changes in neural firing (e.g. Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Moita et al., 2003; Yao and Dan, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies using this approach.

claim: In systems with feedback loops, changes in neural activity at a particular site after learning do not necessarily reflect plasticity in its nominally upstream inputs.
source: However, in systems with feedback loops, the distinction between upstream and downstream is ill-defined, so that changes in the activity of a neuron after learning do not necessarily reflect plasticity in its nominally upstream inputs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the presence of feedback loops, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The Marr-Albus-Ito model assumes a feedforward architecture in which errors are reduced through changes in the synaptic inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: The classic Marr-Albus-Ito model assumes a feedforward architecture in which errors are reduced through changes in the synaptic inputs to Purkinje cells, the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Figure 1C; Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito and Kano, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to the original Marr-Albus-Ito model papers.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) occurs at the excitatory parallel fiber synapses onto Purkinje cells in response to error signals carried by climbing fiber inputs.
source: This is consistent with a large number of studies suggesting that long-term depression (LTD) occurs at the excitatory parallel fiber synapses onto Purkinje cells in response to error signals carried by climbing fiber inputs, effectively implementing reinforcement learning through error-driven plasticity ('parallel fiber-Purkinje cell LTD'; Coesmans et al., 2004; Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Ito and Kano, 1982; Kimpo et al., 2014; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Sakurai, 1987; Silva et al., 2023; Yang and Lisberger, 2013; Yang and Lisberger, 2014, but see Schonewille et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The Miles-Lisberger model proposes that learning-related changes in Purkinje cell firing could be due to feedback of changes occurring outside of the cerebellar cortex.
source: In contrast, later experimental observations raised the possibility that the learning-related changes in Purkinje cell firing could instead be due to feedback of changes occurring outside of the cerebellar cortex ('Miles-Lisberger model', Figure 1D; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger, 1994a; Lisberger et al., 1994c; Lisberger et al., 1994b; Miles and Lisberger, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to the Miles-Lisberger model papers.

claim: The Miles-Lisberger model proposes that parallel fiber-Purkinje cell plasticity within the cerebellar cortex is in the opposite direction (long-term potentiation, LTP) from the LTD predicted by the Marr-Albus-Ito model.
source: Furthermore, these experiments were interpreted as evidence that parallel fiber-Purkinje cell plasticity within the cerebellar cortex was in the opposite direction (long-term potentiation, LTP) from the LTD predicted by the Marr-Albus-Ito model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous experiments cited in the context.

claim: Oculomotor learning provides a powerful experimental system because it regulates a relatively simple transformation from sensory inputs to motor output in a circuit whose anatomy and physiology have been extensively characterized.
source: Oculomotor learning provides a powerful experimental system because it regulates a relatively simple transformation from sensory inputs to motor output in a circuit whose anatomy and physiology have been extensively characterized.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the oculomotor system.

claim: Vestibularly driven eye movements, known as the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), stabilize gaze by counter-rotating the eyes in response to head movement and occur even in complete darkness.
source: Vestibularly driven eye movements, known as the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), stabilize gaze by counter-rotating the eyes in response to head movement and occur even in complete darkness.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the VOR.

claim: Visually driven eye movements, including 'smooth pursuit' eye movements that track a moving target, stabilize images on the retina in response to visual input.
source: Visually driven eye movements, including 'smooth pursuit' eye movements that track a moving target, stabilize images on the retina in response to visual input (Noda and Suzuki, 1979; Rambold et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on smooth pursuit.

claim: Both the visual and vestibular functions of the oculomotor system are remarkably linear.
source: Both the visual and vestibular functions of the oculomotor system are remarkably linear (Bagnall et al., 2008; du Lac and Lisberger, 1995; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; McElvain et al., 2015; Payne et al., 2019; Walter and Khodakhah, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Linear filter models with any level of efference copy input, ranging from a feedback gain of 0 ('No Feedback') to 1 ('Strong Feedback'), closely accounted for the dynamics of neural activity and behavior before learning.
source: Linear filter models with any level of efference copy input, ranging from a feedback gain of 0 ('No Feedback') to 1 ('Strong Feedback'), closely accounted for the dynamics of neural activity and behavior before learning (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by model fits to experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For every stimulus condition, both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models fit the data similarly.
source: For every stimulus condition, both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models fit the data similarly (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by model fits shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strength of efference copy feedback (kPE) to Purkinje cells was unconstrained by a large set of oculomotor data before learning.
source: The strength of efference copy feedback (kPE) to Purkinje cells was thus unconstrained by a large set of oculomotor data before learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results showing degeneracy.

claim: The filters conveying vestibular input and Purkinje cell activity to the brainstem, kEH and kEP, were nearly identical in all models.
source: Some filters did not depend on feedback strength: the filters conveying vestibular input and Purkinje cell activity to the brainstem, kEH and kEP, were nearly identical in all models, indicating that these pathways are well constrained by the data regardless of the strength of efference copy feedback (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The vestibular input filter to Purkinje cells, kPH, changed from small and net negative in the No Feedback model to large and net positive in the Strong Feedback model.
source: The vestibular input filter to Purkinje cells, kPH, changed from small and net negative in the No Feedback model to large and net positive in the Strong Feedback model (Figure 4B, top).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The retinal slip filter varied with feedback strength, changing from acceleration-like to velocity-like as feedback strength decreased.
source: The retinal slip filter also varied with feedback strength, changing from acceleration-like to velocity-like as feedback strength decreased (Figure 4B, bottom; see schematics in Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: In the Strong Feedback model, the efference copy feedback loop forms a temporal integrator that converts acceleration-like inputs to velocity-like outputs.
source: this reflects that, in the Strong Feedback model, the efference copy feedback loop forms a temporal integrator that converts acceleration-like inputs to velocity-like outputs.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: The inferred strength and dynamics of the vestibular and visual inputs to the cerebellar cortex are not well-constrained by this extensive set of data, and varied depending on the assumed strength of efference copy feedback, even before learning.
source: The inferred strength and dynamics of the vestibular and visual inputs to the cerebellar cortex therefore are not well-constrained by this extensive set of data, and varied depending on the assumed strength of efference copy feedback, even before learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results showing degeneracy.

claim: There is a strict degeneracy for some, but not all, parameters in the model.
source: This analysis revealed a strict degeneracy for some, but not all, parameters in the model.
evidence: This is based on mathematical analysis of the simplified model.

claim: The two brainstem pathways, kEH and kEP, were fully constrained, as illustrated by the single minimum in the cost function landscape.
source: Consistent with the results of Figure 4A, the two brainstem pathways, kEH and kEP, were fully constrained, as illustrated by the single minimum in the cost function landscape (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by the cost function analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a degenerate direction in parameter space for the three inputs to Purkinje cells: kPH, kPE, and kPR, as illustrated by the flat valley in the cost function landscape.
source: By contrast, there was a degenerate direction in parameter space for the three inputs to Purkinje cells: kPH, kPE, and kPR, as illustrated by the flat valley in the cost function landscape, where the fit to the data was equally good for a range of different filter strengths (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by the cost function analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The degeneracy reflects that there are only two independently controllable variables, the vestibular and visual target stimuli, yet three unknown input filters.
source: Ultimately, this degeneracy reflects that there are only two independently controllable variables, the vestibular and visual target stimuli, yet three unknown input filters.
evidence: This is a mathematical inference from the model structure.

claim: The vestibular, visual, and efference copy feedback filters to Purkinje cells cannot be fully determined using neural recording and behavioral data alone, but require an additional experimental strategy.
source: The practical implication of this analysis is that the vestibular, visual, and efference copy feedback filters to Purkinje cells cannot be fully determined using neural recording and behavioral data alone, but require an additional experimental strategy.
evidence: This is an inference from the degeneracy analysis.

claim: All models, regardless of the strength of efference copy feedback, successfully reproduced behavioral changes in the VOR after learning.
source: All models, regardless of the strength of efference copy feedback, successfully reproduced behavioral changes in the VOR after learning (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by model fits to behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Each model captured the learned changes in amplitude and phase of the VOR observed in monkeys across stimulus frequencies.
source: Each model captured the learned changes in amplitude and phase of the VOR observed in monkeys across stimulus frequencies (Ramachandran and Lisberger, 2005; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by model fits to experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The net changes in the vestibular filters after learning depended on the level of feedback only for pathways in the cerebellar cortex (kPH) and not in the brainstem (kEH).
source: Similar to the baseline filters before learning, the net changes in the vestibular filters after learning depended on the level of feedback only for pathways in the cerebellar cortex (kPH, Figure 6C) and not in the brainstem (kEH; Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The No Feedback model displayed net depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH), whereas the Strong Feedback model displayed net potentiation at this site.
source: Most strikingly, the No Feedback model displayed net depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH), whereas the Strong Feedback model displayed net potentiation at this site (Figure 6C, right).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a gradual transition between the two extremes, with net depression switching to net potentiation at a feedback gain of around 0.4.
source: Further, there was a gradual transition between the two extremes, with net depression switching to net potentiation at a feedback gain of around 0.4 (Figure 6C, right).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The direction of net plasticity of kPH in each model was necessary, as models failed to reproduce the experimentally observed changes in neural activity during the VOR after learning when the corresponding direction of plasticity was blocked.
source: We confirmed that the direction of net plasticity of kPH in each model was necessary by showing that the models failed to reproduce the experimentally observed changes in neural activity during the VOR after learning when the corresponding direction of plasticity was blocked (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Strong Feedback model displayed depression of an acceleration-like component of kPH, even though the net change at this filter was potentiation.
source: The Strong Feedback model displayed depression of an acceleration-like component of kPH, even though the net change at this filter was potentiation (compare Figure 6C, center with Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 6C and Figure 4C.

claim: Circuits with strong positive feedback can affect steady-state changes in circuit output through changes in dynamics as well as weights.
source: This observation is consistent with the finding that circuits with strong positive feedback can affect steady-state changes in circuit output through changes in dynamics as well as weights (Lisberger and Sejnowski, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models correctly reproduce the observed decrease in Purkinje cell activity, but they use oppositely directed plasticity in the vestibular pathway to do so.
source: Thus, both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models correctly reproduce the observed decrease in Purkinje cell activity, but they use oppositely directed plasticity in the vestibular pathway to do so.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation increases after VOR increase learning.
source: The surprising observation that Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation increases after VOR increase learning was previously interpreted as evidence that the vestibular inputs to Purkinje cells (kPH) must undergo potentiation, rather than depression (Lisberger, 1994a; Miles and Lisberger, 1981).
evidence: This is an experimental observation cited from previous studies.

claim: All models — both those with potentiation and those with depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells, kPH — successfully replicated the increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation.
source: In contrast to the previous interpretation, we found that all models — both those with potentiation and those with depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells, kPH — successfully replicated this increase in Purkinje cell activity (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the Strong Feedback model, the learned increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation is due to potentiation of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH).
source: In the Strong Feedback model, the learned increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation is not surprising: the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH) potentiates, directly driving the increase in firing rate (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: The No Feedback model could reproduce the observed increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation after learning, despite net depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH).
source: More surprisingly, the No Feedback model could also reproduce the observed increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation after learning (Figure 7A and B), despite net depression of the vestibular input to Purkinje cells (kPH) (Figure 6, Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: In the No Feedback model, the increase in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation was accomplished by the external negative feedback of visual error, which drives corrective motor commands.
source: This was accomplished by the second feedback pathway in the circuit: external negative feedback of visual error, which drives corrective motor commands (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The visual feedback loop 'works harder' by increasing its input to Purkinje cells after learning, resulting in more suppression of the brainstem, thereby counteracting the learned increase in the VOR.
source: In essence, the visual feedback loop 'works harder' by increasing its input to Purkinje cells after learning. This results in more suppression of the brainstem, thereby counteracting the learned increase in the VOR.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: Visual negative feedback, regardless of the exact implementation, can cause Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation to change in the opposite direction to that expected from the underlying plasticity of vestibular inputs.
source: Taken together, this analysis demonstrates that visual negative feedback, regardless of the exact implementation, can cause Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation to change in the opposite direction to that expected from the underlying plasticity of vestibular inputs.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: In both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models, the learned increases in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation depended on the existence of plasticity in the direct pathway through the brainstem.
source: In both the No Feedback and Strong Feedback models, the learned increases in Purkinje cell activity during VOR cancellation depended on the existence of plasticity in the direct pathway through the brainstem.
evidence: This is an inference from model simulations where brainstem plasticity was blocked.

claim: When the vestibular input to the brainstem (kEH) was held fixed during learning, motor learning was still successful at the level of the eye movement output during the VOR in the dark, but the learned increase in Purkinje cell firing during VOR cancellation no longer occurred.
source: When the vestibular input to the brainstem (kEH) was held fixed during learning, motor learning was still successful at the level of the eye movement output during the VOR in the dark, but the learned increase in Purkinje cell firing during VOR cancellation no longer occurred (Figure 7B and F, dashed lines).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 7B and F.

claim: In each model, two sites of plasticity—in the brainstem and in the cerebellar cortex—were required to explain the apparent paradox that learning decreases Purkinje cell firing measured during the VOR in the dark but increases firing measured during VOR cancellation.
source: Therefore, in each model, two sites of plasticity—in the brainstem and in the cerebellar cortex—were required to explain the apparent paradox that learning decreases Purkinje cell firing measured during the VOR in the dark but increases firing measured during VOR cancellation.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: A purely feedforward system should only respond briefly to transient stimulation, with a time course dominated by the intrinsic time constants of its neurons and synapses.
source: A purely feedforward system should only respond briefly to transient stimulation, with a time course dominated by the intrinsic time constants of its neurons and synapses.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about feedforward systems.

claim: A system dominated by strong positive feedback should integrate transient stimulation, resulting in a prolonged response.
source: In contrast, a system dominated by strong positive feedback should instead integrate transient stimulation, resulting in a prolonged response (Robinson, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The previously observed degeneracy in the strengths of Purkinje cell inputs is eliminated when a 'Purkinje cell stimulation' condition is added.
source: As a result, sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the previously observed degeneracy in the strengths of Purkinje cell inputs (Figure 5C) is eliminated when a 'Purkinje cell stimulation' condition is added (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Brief stimulus trains (5 pulses at 200 Hz) applied in the absence of visual or vestibular stimulation evoked smooth eye velocity responses that decayed rapidly after stimulus offset.
source: In this experiment, brief stimulus trains (5 pulses at 200 Hz) applied in the absence of visual or vestibular stimulation evoked smooth eye velocity responses that decayed rapidly after stimulus offset (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is experimental data from a previous study, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Models with weak or intermediate feedback produced brief eye velocity responses, akin to the data, whereas models with strong feedback produced prolonged eye velocity responses, unlike the data.
source: Models with weak or intermediate feedback produced brief eye velocity responses, akin to the data, whereas models with strong feedback produced prolonged eye velocity responses, unlike the data (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Feedback in the VOR circuit is relatively weak.
source: this suggests that feedback in this circuit is relatively weak (Figure 8E; see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations of transient stimulation.

claim: Models with weak or no efference copy feedback are compatible with error-driven plasticity in the cerebellar cortex.
source: In this study, we found that only models with weak or no efference copy feedback were compatible with depression of parallel fiber inputs to Purkinje cells, and thus with error-driven plasticity in the cerebellar cortex
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The results reconcile results from VOR learning with other cerebellum-dependent motor learning paradigms, such as eye blink and smooth pursuit learning, where climbing fiber activity has been associated with depression of active parallel fiber inputs.
source: Our study therefore reconciles results from VOR learning with other cerebellum-dependent motor learning paradigms, such as eye blink and smooth pursuit learning, where climbing fiber activity has been less controversially associated with depression of active parallel fiber inputs (Lisberger, 2021; Raymond et al., 1996; Raymond and Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results, supported by citations to other learning paradigms.

claim: Models with strong efference copy feedback predict net potentiation rather than depression of vestibular input to the cerebellar cortex.
source: In contrast, models with strong efference copy feedback predict net potentiation rather than depression of vestibular input to the cerebellar cortex
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The response to transient stimulation of models with relatively strong feedback was incompatible with the experimentally observed response.
source: First, the response to transient stimulation of models with relatively strong feedback was incompatible with the experimentally observed response (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model simulations to experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: The Strong Feedback model with feedback gain equal to 1 is on the brink of instability and requires that any change in the strength of the vestibular input to the Purkinje cells (kPH) must be precisely offset by a change in the strength of the vestibular inputs to the brainstem (kEH) to avoid runaway activity.
source: Second, the Strong Feedback model with feedback gain equal to 1 is on the brink of instability and thus requires that any change in the strength of the vestibular input to the Purkinje cells (kPH) must be precisely offset by a change in the strength of the vestibular inputs to the brainstem (kEH) to avoid runaway activity (Lisberger and Sejnowski, 1992; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics, supported by simulations in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Signals related to motor output have been identified as inputs to the cerebellar cortex.
source: Despite this evidence against models with strong efference copy feedback, there is almost certainly some efference copy input to the cerebellum. Signals related to motor output have been identified as inputs to the cerebellar cortex (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Person, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and the medial vestibular nucleus provide eye movement-related mossy fiber afferents to the cerebellar flocculus.
source: Anatomically, the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and the medial vestibular nucleus provide eye movement-related mossy fiber afferents to the cerebellar flocculus (Escudero et al., 1996b; Escudero et al., 1996a).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The analysis suggests that the functional feedback strength of efference copy pathways is weak.
source: To the extent that true feedback loops are present, our analysis suggests that their functional feedback strength is weak (Figure 6C and Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results shown in Figures 6C and 8B-C.

claim: Studies of cerebellar learning suggest that memories rapidly form in the cerebellar cortex before being gradually transferred to the brainstem or cerebellar nuclei.
source: Studies of cerebellar learning suggest that memories rapidly form in the cerebellar cortex before being gradually transferred to the brainstem or cerebellar nuclei (Kassardjian et al., 2005; Shutoh et al., 2006; reviewed in De Zeeuw et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on systems consolidation.

claim: Systems consolidation from a faster-learning site to a slower-learning site has been shown theoretically to mitigate the 'stability-plasticity dilemma' of allowing fast learning without over-writing old memories.
source: Such consolidation from a faster-learning site to a slower-learning site is known as systems consolidation and has been shown theoretically to mitigate the 'stability-plasticity dilemma' of allowing fast learning without over-writing old memories.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about systems consolidation.

claim: The model presented represents a single time point of learning, with most of the post-learning experimental data coming from animals that were trained on previous days as well as the day of recording.
source: The model presented here represents a single time point of learning, with most of the post-learning experimental data coming from animals that were trained on previous days as well as the day of recording (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data used in the study.

claim: Before consolidation, learning-related decreases in Purkinje cell firing during the VOR may be supported solely by plasticity in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Before consolidation, learning-related decreases in Purkinje cell firing during the VOR may be supported solely by plasticity in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the model.

claim: If learning-related decreases in Purkinje cell firing during the VOR are supported solely by plasticity in the cerebellar cortex before consolidation, then 'paradoxical' increases in Purkinje cell responses occurring during VOR cancellation would not be observed at the earliest stages of learning before brainstem plasticity has occurred.
source: If this is the case, then our model predicts that 'paradoxical' increases in Purkinje cell responses occurring during VOR cancellation (Figure 7) would not be observed at the earliest stages of learning before brainstem plasticity has occurred.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the model.

claim: In complex biological circuits, many different configurations of biological parameters can enable a circuit to accomplish the same task, resulting in degeneracy in the relation between model parameters and circuit output, known as 'sloppiness in model fits'.
source: In complex biological circuits, many different configurations of biological parameters can enable a circuit to accomplish the same task. This results in degeneracy in the relation between model parameters and circuit output, known as 'sloppiness in model fits' (Bittner et al., 2021; Costa et al., 2013; Fisher et al., 2013; Foster et al., 1993; Goldman et al., 2001; Gonçalves et al., 2020; O'Leary and Marder, 2016; Prinz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work on sloppiness in models.

claim: The presence of multiple feedforward and feedback pathways converging on the same site can lead to sloppiness in inferring the sites and signs of plasticity.
source: We show that the presence of multiple feedforward and feedback pathways converging on the same site can lead to sloppiness in inferring the sites and signs of plasticity
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: Additional data from perturbations may constrain the most fundamental aspects of sloppiness in model fits.
source: but that additional data from perturbations may constrain the most fundamental aspects of this sloppiness.
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis with transient stimulation.

claim: Previous studies used multiple linear regression analysis to assess the strength of efference copy feedback by fitting Purkinje cell activity to linear combinations of position, velocity, and/or acceleration of vestibular input, retinal slip, and eye movement.
source: In such analyses, Purkinje cell activity was fit to linear combinations of position, velocity, and/or acceleration of vestibular input, retinal slip, and eye movement ('efference copy input'; Blazquez et al., 2003; Hirata and Highstein, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies found non-zero values for the coefficients representing eye velocity, which has been interpreted as evidence for efference copy feedback to Purkinje cells.
source: These analyses found non-zero values for the coefficients representing eye velocity, which has been interpreted as evidence for efference copy feedback to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a description of previous interpretations of experimental results.

claim: Previous regression models are a special case of the more general linear filter models analyzed in this study, for which there is an inherent non-identifiability of the inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: More fundamentally, these models are a special case of the more general linear filter models analyzed here, for which there is an inherent non-identifiability of the inputs to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: The correlational plasticity rule applied to the efference copy pathway predicts net potentiation of kPE for learned increases in the VOR.
source: Hence, activation of parallel fibers carrying efference copy signals should be accompanied by little or no climbing fiber activity, which in vitro has been shown to induce potentiation of the parallel fibers inputs to Purkinje cells (Crepel and Jaillard, 1991; Suvrathan et al., 2016). Thus, we predict net potentiation of kPE for learned increases in the VOR.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the correlational plasticity rule and in vitro studies.

claim: The correlational plasticity rule applied to the efference copy pathway predicts net depression of kPE for learned decreases in the VOR.
source: Applying similar logic to learned decreases in the VOR predicts net depression of kPE.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the correlational plasticity rule.

claim: Changes in kPE would lead to alterations of VOR dynamics, as well as amplitude, due to changing the strength of the efference copy feedback loop.
source: Changes in kPE would also lead to alterations of VOR dynamics, as well as amplitude, due to changing the strength of the efference copy feedback loop (Lisberger and Sejnowski, 1992).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the model, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: For the visual pathway, the correlational learning rule predicts potentiation of kPR during both learned increases and decreases in the VOR.
source: For the visual pathway, the correlational learning rule predicts potentiation of kPR during both learned increases and decreases in the VOR, because visual error simultaneously drives climbing fiber and parallel fiber input in the same direction, so parallel fiber-climbing fiber correlations are independent of the sign of visual error.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the correlational plasticity rule.

claim: Potentiation of kPR may explain the increase in Purkinje cell firing during smooth pursuit that is observed after both directions of VOR learning.
source: This may explain the increase in Purkinje cell firing during smooth pursuit that is observed after both directions of VOR learning (Blazquez et al., 2003; Lisberger et al., 1994b; Miles et al., 1980).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: The model is agnostic to the biological mechanism by which the vestibular inputs to Purkinje cells undergo net 'depression'.
source: Our model is agnostic to the biological mechanism by which the vestibular inputs to Purkinje cells undergo net 'depression'.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's assumptions.

claim: Instead of the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse undergoing LTD, the parallel fiber-interneuron synapse or the interneuron-Purkinje cell synapse could undergo LTP.
source: For example, instead of the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapse undergoing LTD, the parallel fiber-interneuron synapse or the interneuron-Purkinje cell synapse could undergo LTP (Carey, 2011; Jörntell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Instead of ipsiversive vestibular inputs undergoing LTD, contraversive vestibular inputs could undergo LTP.
source: Additionally, instead of ipsiversive vestibular inputs undergoing LTD, contraversive vestibular inputs could undergo LTP, since there are two cerebellar flocculi located bilaterally which converge to move the eyes.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Models with weak efference copy feedback are consistent with multiple plasticity mechanisms, including a contribution to VOR learning from LTP.
source: Therefore, our models with weak efference copy feedback are consistent with multiple plasticity mechanisms, including a contribution to VOR learning from LTP (Boyden et al., 2004; De Zeeuw, 2021; du Lac et al., 1995; Titley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results, supported by citations to studies on LTP.

claim: Visual input was modeled only to the cerebellar cortex, motivated by studies that show large decreases in the amplitude of smooth pursuit eye movements following lesions of the floccular complex.
source: We modeled visual input only to the cerebellar cortex, motivated by studies that show large decreases in the amplitude of smooth pursuit eye movements following lesions of the floccular complex (Belton and McCrea, 2000; Burde et al., 1975; Estanol et al., 1979; Rambold et al., 2002; Westheimer and Blair, 1974; Zee et al., 1981).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: There is some anatomical evidence for direct visual input to the brainstem.
source: There is some anatomical evidence for direct visual input to the brainstem as well (Balaban, 1983)
evidence: Supported by citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The functional impact of efference copy feedback to Purkinje cells could be more directly assessed by comparing the motor response to Purkinje cell stimulation in the presence versus absence of parallel fiber input.
source: The functional impact of such feedback to Purkinje cells could be more directly assessed by comparing the motor response to Purkinje cell stimulation in the presence versus absence of parallel fiber input.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental test.

claim: One study in mice blocked granule cell activity, which appeared to have little effect on the dynamics of the motor response to Purkinje cell stimulation, supportive of a weak feedback model in mice.
source: One study in mice did just that by blocking granule cell activity, which appeared to have little effect on the dynamics of the motor response to Purkinje cell stimulation, supportive of a weak feedback model in mice, although this was not quantified (Wada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study in mice.

claim: If VOR cancellation is measured immediately after training, before consolidation has occurred, then paradoxical increases in Purkinje cell activity will no longer be observed, according to the weak feedback models.
source: Finally, as described above, our weak feedback models predict that if VOR cancellation is measured immediately after training, before consolidation has occurred, then paradoxical increases in Purkinje cell activity will no longer be observed.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the model.
